newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says ECB could use money or inflation targets.
newsitem.headline: EMI says ECB could use money or inflation targets.

text.p: The future European central bank could use either monetary targeting or inflation targeting to steer its monetary policy, and must decide itself which guide to adopt, the European Monetary Institute said.

In a report published on Friday, the Frankfurt-based forerunner to the European Central Bank said that it had considered five possible monetary strategies that the ECB could adopt, and had eliminated the use of exchange rate targeting, interest rate pegging or nominal income targeting.

It said these did not fit in with the general principles it had set for the ECB's strategy -- which included the need for an effective, accountable and transparent policy, taking an independent, medium-term orientation and using the experience gained by national central banks (NCBs) before the start of EMU.

"Taking into account a number of guiding principles...and considering the environment likely to prevail in the euro area, the list of potential candidate strategies has been narrowed down to two, namely monetary targeting and direct inflation targeting," the EMI said.
It said the use of exchange rate targeting had been ruled out on the grounds that this could be at odds with the central bank's top priority -- maintenance of price stability.

"An exchange rate objective is not considered appropriate since, for an area as potentially large as the euro area, such an approach might be inconsistent with the internal goal of price stability," the EMI said.

It added that the high level of intra-EU trade meant that a exchange rate developments would "most likely constitute less of a concern for the conduct of monetary policy than is currently the case for many NCBs".

The concept of interest rate pegging posed a problem in identifying the appropriate rate to target, while nominal income would be difficult for the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) to control, the EMI said.
The EMI noted that the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union made absolutely clear that the ECB had to see price stability as its top priority.
"As regards the final objective itself, the Treaty provides unambiguous guidance that 'the primary objective of the ESCB shall be to maintain price stability'," it said.
Declining to come down firmly in favour of either monetary or inflation targeting, the EMI said that this decision must be left to the ECB itself, once it is established in 1998.
It added that although there were clear theoretical differences between these two approaches "the borderlines between the two (are) sometimes less distinct than in theory".

Playing down the differences between the two strategies, the EMI said, "Overall...the similarities in the behaviour of central banks that pursue these two strategies are greater than the differences."
"Regardless of their choice of strategy, they all monitor a wide and similar set of economic and financial variables as indicators in the determination of the monetary policy stance."
When deciding which strategy to adopt, the ECB would have to take into account the general conditions prevailing at the start of the third stage of monetary union, the EMI said.

While several factors spoke in favour of monetary targeting -- including the fact that it is the practice followed by the German Bundesbank -- it was not yet clear whether there was money demand in the euro area would demonstrate the long-term stability needed for the success of the strategy.
"Uncertainty concerning the empirical properties of money demand in the euro area in Stage Three is the main argument against a monetary targeting strategy," the EMI said.
But similarly, with an inflation strategy, a link would have to be established between current conditions and future inflation to ensure the success of the strategy.

"It should be noted, however, that to be successful inflation targeting also requires stable relationships between various economic and financial indicators, on the one hand, and future inflation, on the other," it said.
The EMI and the national contral banks were undertaking preparatory work to ensure that the ESCB would have the statistical and analytical infrastructure at its disposal to pursue either strategy.
--Janet Northcote, Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
